messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eleanor was 77, an environmental scientist who had spent decades studying soil composition in remote forest plots, but the rape had happened when she was thirty-three, after a fieldwork conference. She had accepted a ride back to her hotel from a male colleague she trusted, and in the room he had forced himself on her. For years afterward she told herself she should have known—she should have locked the door, should have worn something less friendly, should have said no more firmly. That self-blame hardened into a fixed belief: you can never know who will harm you, and the safest assumption is that any man, given the chance, might become a threat. Because of this belief, every male presence now felt charged. When a junior researcher offered a collegial hug after a successful lab day, Eleanor’s chest tightened not with warmth but with alarm—she had come to see physical affection as a prelude to violation, and she pulled back before the embrace could land.

Her threat monitoring had become automatic. In any room she entered first, her eyes scanned for exits; she always sat with her back to a wall and her chair placed so she could see the door. Sudden movements from others put her immediately on guard—a coworker reaching quickly for a file made her flinch. At home she listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering, checking locks twice before bed. This constant vigilance fed her negative appraisals: the more she watched for danger, the more dangerous the world seemed, and the more she blamed herself for not having been watchful enough during the assault. It also sharpened her triggers. Being alone with a man in a closed office now felt like a setup for repetition, and any sexual situation—a scene in a TV show, a passing remark—made her skin crawl with shame for what her body had endured.

To manage the relentless threat, Eleanor had developed strategies that only deepened her isolation. She avoided eye contact with nearly everyone, especially men, because meeting someone’s gaze felt like an invitation she could not risk. In meetings she stared at her notes. She also avoided open spaces: she had stopped going to field sites years ago, telling her supervisor she preferred lab work, but the truth was that exposed areas made her feel impossibly vulnerable, as if any man could approach from any direction. These avoidances kept her from ever learning that a male colleague could be safe, which reinforced her belief that danger was everywhere and that she had somehow caused the original event by not being more guarded. Each time she took a different hallway to avoid passing a group of men, her sense of threat increased—the very act of avoiding confirmed that the threat was real.

Prevention rumination consumed her evenings. She would replay the night of the rape, trying to find the exact moment she could have changed course—she should have taken a taxi, should not have accepted that last drink. She blamed her own actions so thoroughly that her body shame grew tangled with it: she felt disgust for the body that had been used, and for the body that, in her mind, had not fought hard enough. The causal loop tightened. Her threat monitoring made her avoid; her avoidance made her more afraid; her fear made every male presence, every gesture of affection, every accidental intimacy feel like an ambush waiting to happen.

At work she used to lead field expeditions, but now she only took indoor assignments. The consequence was concrete: she was passed over for a promotion to senior researcher because she refused to mentor a promising male graduate student one-on-one. Her colleagues thought she was difficult; she knew she was terrified.

What finally brought her to seek help was a younger woman in her department who was assaulted on a night out. Eleanor heard the news and spent the next week unable to sleep, replaying her own attack as if it were yesterday, and for the first time she saw in the younger woman’s face the same self-blame she had carried for decades. She walked into the clinic with her hands shaking, afraid that talking about it would make everything real again, but even more afraid of spending whatever years she had left watching every doorway and wondering who might harm her next.
